item.title: The Inverse Mapper Problem for Two-Dimensional Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.30380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mapper algorithm is a popular graphical tool for data visualization and exploration in topological data analysis (TDA). It takes as input a data set $X$ and returns a graph that aims to capture the underlying topological features of these data. The Mapper algorithm has several parameters that need to be specified by the user: a $\textit{filter function}$ $f:X\to Y$ where $X$ is often a point cloud data set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $Y$ is the $\textit{reference space}$ that is often a lower dimensional Euclidean space, a $\textit{cover}$ of $f(X)$, and a $\textit{clustering algorithm}$ that is applied to the pre-image of each element in the cover. In this paper, we consider the following question: What graphs can occur as the output of the Mapper algorithm? It is known that when $Y=\mathbb{R}^3$, any graph can be a Mapper graph. In this work, we focus on a more practical case where the filter function is $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$. We consider two different scenarios. In the first scenario, we fix the parameters of the Mapper algorithm, but vary the data. This way we characterize exactly the graphs that can occur for several choices of parameters. In the second scenario, we fix the data set but vary the parameters. This can be seen as a way to understand how much the output can differ depending on the choices of parameters.In both settings, we find close connections to classical topics in graph drawing.
item.dc:creator: Robin Belton, Patrick Schnider

item.title: Beyond Homology: Non-Abelian and Orientability Invariants Sensitivity in Cellular Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.31234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) architectures are typically evaluated on synthetic complex pairs that differ in a target invariant. Yet, whether a model recovers that invariant or an artifact of the chosen discretization is seldom audited. To examine this, we design and test pairs of complexes that look identical to standard homological and local message-passing tests, have the same Hasse graphs, yet differ in the target invariant. We study two beyond-homology regimes: nonAbelian fundamental-group structure and homotopy-matched orientability. For the former, we construct genus-2 pairs that match homology, cell statistics, local incidence profiles, and rank-colored Hasse 1-WL behavior while differing in their fundamental groups. For the latter, we evaluate punctured torus-Klein bottle pairs and show that distance, boundary, cycle, and spectral signals can confound apparent orientability detection, motivating stronger matched controls. Under the tested settings, subcomplex-lifted architectures separate some pairs beyond the matched homological, local-incidence, and Hasse 1-WL controls, while a depth sweep reveals an empirical depth-dependent trend without establishing a general barrier or direct computation of the target invariants. These results show that claims of topological expressivity must be stated relative to the model representation, explicitly controlled information channels, and the precise scope of the benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Raghuwansh Raj, George Panagopoulos, Jun Pang

item.title: Bridging persistence of discrete and continuous 1D maps: Total variation, permutation equivalence, and diagonal affine transformations
item.description: arXiv:2610.31391v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fundamental to the field of topological signal processing (TSP) is the \textit{persistence diagram} (PD), or barcode, of a signal, which gives noise-resistant measures of topologically significant features as distinct from noise. Existing literature proves that the total persistence computed from these diagrams is equal to the total variation, for certain continuous signals on compact domains. We provide a closed formula for this shared quantity, and generalize to all continuous and discrete functions on bounded domains, and to certain functions on non-compact 1D manifolds. Extending the identification of continuous and discrete persistence, we investigate the similarities of functions with the same PDs, and prove that, for any $n$, the persistence diagram can be calculated as a function of the sequence of critical values; we compute these formulas for $n \leq 6$. Finally, we examine which function transformations cause predictable changes in the PD of the transformed function, characterizing affine and linear transformations.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Blake, Firas A. Khasawneh

item.title: Coresets for $k$-Means: When Does Uniform Sampling Suffice?
item.description: arXiv:2610.31491v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data summarization techniques, such as coresets, are essential for scaling clustering algorithms to massive datasets. We study uniform sampling, which is an extremely simple and ultra-efficient method to construct coresets, in the context of weak, stable, and strong coresets for the $k$-means problem in Hilbert space. We begin with the fundamental case $k=1$, and establish matching upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of stable and weak coresets, finding that the two notions require different sample complexities. As a consequence, we obtain tight bounds for stable $1$-median coresets in $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ (and thus also Kendall--tau and Jaccard metrics), removing the dimension dependence of Carmel and Krauthgamer (ICLR 2026). Our analysis is substantially simpler than prior work and reduces to bounding the deviation of the sample mean. For the general $k$-means problem on $\rho$-separated instances, a well-studied structural assumption on the input, we show that uniform sampling yields a stable coreset for all $O(1)$-approximate solutions, and a strong coreset if the instance additionally has bounded kurtosis. In all these results, the sample complexity is independent of the dimension and the instance size.
item.dc:creator: Amir Carmel, Robert Krauthgamer

item.title: Approximation algorithm for mixed volumes of a constant number of convex bodies
item.description: arXiv:2610.08248v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the computation of mixed volumes of convex sets given as rational subspace sections of bodies described by membership oracles. The sets need not have nonempty interior. For positive multiplicities $\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k=n$, we give a randomized algorithm that computes a relative $\varepsilon$-approximation with probability at least $1-\delta$. Its running time is polynomial in Gurvits' factor $\Gamma_\alpha=(n^n/n!)\prod_i\alpha_i!/\alpha_i^{\alpha_i}$, the input presentation length, and $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and linear in $1+\log\delta^{-1}$, with degree independent of $k$. The running-time bound holds for every choice of the random bits, and zero mixed volumes are detected exactly. We extend the capacity-scaling and sampling method of Narayanan--Roy by using rational projections and a smooth mixed Monge--Amp\`ere representation. In particular, the algorithm runs in randomized polynomial time when the number of distinct convex sets is bounded above by a constant.
item.dc:creator: Hariharan Narayanan

item.title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics
item.description: arXiv:2403.17147v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks. Yet swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded. Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm's geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation. These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures. We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation. We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse-connectivity conditions. Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.
item.dc:creator: Leo Cazenille, Nicolas Lobato-Dauzier, Alessia Loi, Loona Macabre, Mika Ito, Olivier Marchal, Soo-Hyeon Kim, Nathanael Aubert-Kato, Nicolas Bredeche, Anthony J. Genot

item.title: Logarithmic edge-length ratios for planar drawings of 2-trees
item.description: arXiv:2610.28030v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For a planar graph $G$ with at least one edge, let $\rho(G)$ be the infimum of the ratio of the longest to the shortest edge length over all planar straight-line drawings of $G$. We prove that every $n$-vertex $2$-tree $G$ satisfies $\rho(G)\le4+5\lfloor\log_2(2n-3)\rfloor$. This improves the known $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound and, together with the lower bound of Bla\v{z}ej, Fiala and Liotta, shows that the maximum of $\rho(G)$ over $n$-vertex $2$-trees is $\Theta(\log n)$. The proof adapts Biedl's recursive bar construction using nonintegral heights and applies a height-preserving straightening theorem.
item.dc:creator: Zahra Sabaei, Fatemeh Emami, Yasmin Tousinejad
